messages.content:
You turn an incident review, written by a data-centre operator's own engineers after they solved a problem, into proposed changes to an "intelligence pill": a governed card of know-how that a facility team applies during the first hour of a cooling or power event.

You work only from the numbered sentences you are given. You add nothing from general knowledge.

Each change is one of:
- add_rule: a new piece of judgement. "when" = observable conditions a duty team could check; "then" = concrete actions; "why" = the reason the review gives; optional "escalate" = who must be called and on what trigger.
- amend_rule: add conditions or actions to an existing rule (give its rule_id) because this review sharpens it.
- add_guardrail: something the team or an assistant must not do or must not rely on.
- ask_expert: a question the review leaves open that an expert must answer before the pill can be trusted on it (for example a threshold, a time limit, who decides). Use this instead of guessing.

Hard rules:
1. Every add_rule, amend_rule and add_guardrail lists "evidence": the ids of the sentences that support it, copied exactly as they appear in review_sentences (for example "AZ-SCUS-2018:S9", with no prefix). No evidence, no change.
2. Never write a number (temperature, minutes, counts) that is not in a cited sentence. If a number matters but is missing, use ask_expert.
3. Write rules about facility operations (power, cooling, staffing, procedures, controls). Ignore cloud-software recovery details.
4. Prefer judgement over description: what an experienced engineer would check or do next, and why, not a retelling of the event.
5. If "focus_findings" are given, they are what the current pill failed to anticipate in this incident; make sure each one is either covered by a change or turned into ask_expert.

Reply with JSON only: {"changes": [ ... ]}. Shapes:
{"op":"add_rule","title":"...","when":["..."],"then":["..."],"why":"...","escalate":{"to":"...","trigger":"..."},"evidence":["<id copied from review_sentences>"]}
{"op":"amend_rule","rule_id":"R-001","add_when":["..."],"add_then":["..."],"why":"...","evidence":["<id copied from review_sentences>"]}
{"op":"add_guardrail","text":"...","evidence":["<id copied from review_sentences>"]}
{"op":"ask_expert","question":"...","why":"..."}

{"incident":{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022","title":"Redundant cooling systems fail together during record heat (Google Cloud, London)","operator":"Google Cloud","site":"europe-west2-a, one data center (London)"},"review_sentences":[{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S3","text":"On Tuesday, 19 July 2022 at 06:33 US/Pacific, a simultaneous failure of multiple, redundant cooling systems in one of the data centers that hosts the zone europe-west2-a impacted multiple Google Cloud services."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S16","text":"Google engineers powered down the data center that hosted a portion of the impacted zone europe-west2-a on Tuesday, 19 July 2022 at 10:05 US/Pacific while the cooling system was repaired."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S28","text":"Google is conducting a detailed analysis of the systems and processes involved in both the cooling failure and the service recovery, with specific followup AIs identified below."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S30","text":"One of the data centers that hosts zone europe-west2-a could not maintain a safe operating temperature due to a simultaneous failure of multiple, redundant cooling systems combined with the extraordinarily high outside temperatures."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S31","text":"We powered down this part of the zone to prevent an even longer outage or damage to machines."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S34","text":"Google engineers were alerted to an issue affecting two cooling systems in one of the data centers that hosts europe-west2-a on Tuesday, 19 July 2022 at 06:33 US/Pacific and began an investigation."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S35","text":"Engineers were engaged at 07:02 and began assessing viable mitigations."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S36","text":"At 10:05, our engineers decided to power down servers in the impacted data center within europe-west2-a to prevent an even longer outage and further impact to infrastructure in the zone."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S42","text":"We will investigate and develop more advanced methods to progressively decrease the thermal load within a single data center space, reducing the probability that a full shutdown is required."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S46","text":"Google engineers are actively conducting a detailed analysis of the cooling system failure that triggered this incident."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S47","text":"Google engineers will be conducting an audit of cooling system equipment and standards across the data centers that house Google Cloud globally."},{"id":"GCP-LDN-2022:S52","text":"As data center temperatures started to increase, on Tuesday, 19 July 2022 at 08:06 US/Pacific Compute Engine terminated 42% of the Preemptible VMs (PVMs) across the europe-west2 region to reduce thermal load in zone europe-west2-a and ensure space for zonal failover activities in zones europe-west2-b and europe-west2-c."}],"current_pill":{"pill":"dc-cooling-loss@1.1.0","scope":{"assets":["data halls cooled by chilled-water plant (chillers, pumps, chilled-water loop)","utility and generator power feeding that plant"],"not_for":["IT service recovery and failover","fire suppression and life safety (follow the site emergency plan)"]},"rules":[{"id":"R-001","title":"Treat utility voltage swells as a cooling-plant threat, not just a power-transfer event","when":["storms are active in the area and the utility feed shows voltage sags or swells","a portion of the datacenter has transferred from utility power to generator power"],"then":["immediately verify that mechanical cooling systems are still running, rather than assuming surge suppressors protected them","if mechanical cooling has shut down, treat the datacenter as being on a load-dependent thermal buffer and start planning for its depletion","transfer the rest of the datacenter to generators to stabilize the power supply while storms are still active"],"why":"Voltage swells triggered a transfer to generator power and also shut down the mechanical cooling systems despite surge suppressors being in place; the site initially survived only on a load-dependent thermal buffer.","escalate":{"to":"facility operations lead and cooling plant engineer","trigger":"mechanical cooling confirmed shut down while storms remain active in the area"}},{"id":"R-002","title":"Act on thermal buffer depletion before automated shutdowns begin","when":["mechanical cooling is down and the datacenter is running on its load-dependent thermal buffer","datacenter temperature is approaching safe operational thresholds"],"then":["treat the thermal buffer as a finite resource and act before it is depleted","expect that once the buffer is gone, temperature will exceed safe operational thresholds and automated device shutdown will begin","recognize that in parts of the datacenter temperature can rise so quickly that hardware is damaged before it can shut down"],"why":"Once the thermal buffer was depleted the datacenter exceeded safe operational thresholds and automated shutdown began, but temperatures rose so quickly in places that some hardware was damaged before it could shut down.","escalate":{"to":"incident commander","trigger":"thermal buffer depletion is imminent or automated shutdowns have started"}},{"id":"R-003","title":"Treat a control-system failover as a cooling-availability event, not a routine maintenance action","when":["the datacenter control system is in the process of failing away from one of its control hosts","the control system is exchanging state information with other control systems and with cooling equipment and temperature sensors"],"then":["treat the failover as a period of elevated risk to cooling availability and watch the cooling plant directly, not only the control system","expect that a fault in the control system logic during this exchange can make the control system unresponsive","verify that cooling systems have actually entered their designed maximum-cooling fallback rather than assuming the fallback engaged"],"why":"The control system was mid-failover when a bug in third-party control logic caused excessive interactions with datacenter devices and left the control system unresponsive; the designed fallback to maximum cooling did not engage everywhere.","escalate":{"to":"facility operations lead and cooling plant engineer","trigger":"control system failover in progress or control system confirmed unresponsive"}},{"id":"R-004","title":"When the control system is down, work the cooling chain by hand and reset the PLCs","when":["the datacenter control system is unavailable and operators have minimum visibility into cooling health and state","cooling has not transitioned to maximum cooling or purge mode in part of the datacenter"],"then":["do not wait for the control system to come back; manually investigate the affected cooling equipment","check the Programmable Logic Controllers controlling the air handling units, since they can be unresponsive even when the control system is the visible failure","reset the affected equipment and PLCs and place them into a maximum cooling configuration","confirm cooling is restored and temperatures are falling before standing down"],"why":"The control system was unavailable, purge failed, and recovery required manually investigating and resetting all affected equipment into maximum cooling; the unresponsive PLCs controlling some air handling units were what prevented both default cooling and purge from working.","escalate":{"to":"incident commander","trigger":"temperatures are rising and servers have begun powering off"}}],"guardrails":[{"id":"G-001","text":"Do not rely on surge suppressors alone to keep mechanical cooling available during utility voltage swells; the review records that cooling shut down despite surge suppressors being in place."},{"id":"G-002","text":"Do not assume onsite redundancies make customer workloads safe from a datacenter cooling failure; the review states there are scenarios in which a cooling failure can impact customer workloads in the affected datacenter."},{"id":"G-003","text":"Do not treat purge mode as a guaranteed independent fallback while PLCs may be unresponsive; the review records that purge failed in the affected areas because the PLC controllers were unresponsive, and that purge is only being modified to bypass PLCs in newer designs."},{"id":"G-004","text":"Do not rely on the datacenter control system for visibility into cooling health during a control-system failure; the review records that the operations team had minimum visibility into cooling health and state while the control system was unavailable."},{"id":"G-005","text":"Do not assume the control-system failover mode that triggered this bug is available; the review records that this failover mode has been disabled in the interim to prevent recurrence."}]},"focus_findings":[{"id":"F1","kind":"root_cause","text":"One of the data centers that hosts zone europe-west2-a could not maintain a safe operating temperature due to a simultaneous failure of multiple, redundant cooling systems combined with the extraordinarily high outside temperatures."},{"id":"F2","kind":"response","text":"As data center temperatures started to increase, on Tuesday, 19 July 2022 at 08:06 US/Pacific Compute Engine terminated 42% of the Preemptible VMs (PVMs) across the europe-west2 region to reduce thermal load in zone europe-west2-a and ensure space for zonal failover activities in zones europe-west2-b and europe-west2-c."},{"id":"F3","kind":"response","text":"At 10:05, our engineers decided to power down servers in the impacted data center within europe-west2-a to prevent an even longer outage and further impact to infrastructure in the zone."},{"id":"F4","kind":"remediation","text":"We will investigate and develop more advanced methods to progressively decrease the thermal load within a single data center space, reducing the probability that a full shutdown is required."},{"id":"F5","kind":"remediation","text":"Google engineers will be conducting an audit of cooling system equipment and standards across the data centers that house Google Cloud globally."},{"id":"F6","kind":"impact","text":"The total duration of the cooling system failure impact was 4 hours, 8 minutes."}]}
